messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Multivariate multilevel logistic regression (Proportional data)
parts:
You mean values of the parameter "p" or do you mean "p values",
the stats concept?

I'm also not sure what you mean by "log logit likelihood".
I see that there's a comment with that content in your file.
All you need to do is give Stan the log-odds as a parameter
to binomial_logit, because

binomial_logit(N, alpha) =def= binomial(N, inv_logit(alpha))

Stan doesn't (at least yet) discriminate between the prior
and the likelihood --- they're all just part of the model.

As to suggestions for your model, you need to be careful with
arithmetic depending on where your parameters go. Stan has
more stable built-in functions for things like log(1 + x) [log1p]
and for addition on the log scale (log_sum_exp). You probably
don't want to use what you have:
> increment_log_prob( Numer[j,i]*log(exp(beta0[ID[j],i]))-Deno[j,i]*log(1+exp(beta0[CCG[j],i])));

First of all, log(exp(a)) = a, whereas exp(a) is prone to overflow.
We also have built in:

log1p_exp(a) =def= log(1 + exp(a))

These are common operations.

We are also not recommending inverse Wishart priors --- see the
manual for the scaled correlation matrices we do recommend --- but
this is a modeling choice. Stan doesn't need to rely on conjugacy
for the multivariate distributions.

- Bob

Maybe someone else can jump in here --- I don't know
what that means.

I suspect what is sought here is a model in which multiple binary outcomes are modeled as correlated through a common matrix of varying intercepts. The intercepts are sampled from a multi_normal, but then pushed through logistic transform to get probabilities for each outcome for each cluster.

For example (the following is not Stan code!):

y1_ij ~ binomial( n1 , p1_ij )
y2_ij ~ binomial( n2 , p2_ij )
logit(p1_ij) = a1j
logit(p2_ij) = a2j
(a1j,a2j) ~ multi_normal( (a1,a2) , Sigma )
// + priors

So the outcomes y1,y2 end up correlated through the varying effect matrix, but are different outcome variables. The cluster indexed by j is measured for both y1 and y2.

I was working on something like this recently for a plant biologist, who has thousands of replicate plants and three outcomes measured per plant (possibly repeated at different growth points). One thing of interest is the correlation structure among the outcomes as a function of treatment, so I used something like the above to do it. Here's the basic Stan mode code I used, which might help Vera, or at least clarify the issue. (NB: this code isn't optimized yet. It could be faster, I'm sure.)

data{
    int N;              // number of plants
    real Mass[N];       // outcome variable 1
    int Ripe[N];        // outcome variable 2
    int Seed[N];        // outcome variable 3
}
parameters{
    vector[3] alpha;    // means of each outcome across plants
    vector[3] aj[N];    // plant specific means, 3 for each of N plants
    real<lower=0> M_sd;
    vector<lower=0>[3] sigma;    // standard deviation of each outcome
    corr_matrix[3] Rho;  // correlation matrix
}
model{
    // temp variables
    matrix[3,3] Sigma;    // composed covariance matrix
    
    // priors
    Rho ~ lkj_corr(2);
    sigma ~ cauchy(0,2);
    alpha ~ normal(1,100);
    M_sd ~ cauchy(0,1);
    
    // plant means
    Sigma <- diag_matrix(sigma) * Rho * diag_matrix(sigma);
    for ( j in 1:N ) aj[j] ~ multi_normal( rep_vector(0,3) , Sigma );
    
    // likelihoods
    for ( j in 1:N ) {
        Mass[j] ~ normal( alpha[1] + aj[j,1] , M_sd );
        Ripe[j] ~ poisson_log( alpha[2] + aj[j,2] );
        Seed[j] ~ poisson_log( alpha[3] + aj[j,3] );
    }
}

I suspect what is sought here is a model in which multiple binary outcomes are modeled as correlated through a common matrix of varying intercepts. The intercepts are sampled from a multi_normal, but then pushed through logistic transform to get probabilities for each outcome for each cluster.

For example (the following is not Stan code!):

y1_ij ~ binomial( n1 , p1_ij )
y2_ij ~ binomial( n2 , p2_ij )
logit(p1_ij) = a1j
logit(p2_ij) = a2j
(a1j,a2j) ~ multi_normal( (a1,a2) , Sigma )
// + priors

So the outcomes y1,y2 end up correlated through the varying effect matrix, but are different outcome variables. The cluster indexed by j is measured for both y1 and y2.

I was working on something like this recently for a plant biologist, who has thousands of replicate plants and three outcomes measured per plant (possibly repeated at different growth points). One thing of interest is the correlation structure among the outcomes as a function of treatment, so I used something like the above to do it. Here's the basic Stan mode code I used, which might help Vera, or at least clarify the issue. (NB: this code isn't optimized yet. It could be faster, I'm sure.)

data{
    int N;              // number of plants
    real Mass[N];       // outcome variable 1
    int Ripe[N];        // outcome variable 2
    int Seed[N];        // outcome variable 3
}
parameters{
    vector[3] alpha;    // means of each outcome across plants
    vector[3] aj[N];    // plant specific means, 3 for each of N plants
    real<lower=0> M_sd;
    vector<lower=0>[3] sigma;    // standard deviation of each outcome
    corr_matrix[3] Rho;  // correlation matrix
}
model{
    // temp variables
    matrix[3,3] Sigma;    // composed covariance matrix
    
    // priors
    Rho ~ lkj_corr(2);
    sigma ~ cauchy(0,2);
    alpha ~ normal(1,100);
    M_sd ~ cauchy(0,1);
    
    // plant means
    Sigma <- diag_matrix(sigma) * Rho * diag_matrix(sigma);
    for ( j in 1:N ) aj[j] ~ multi_normal( rep_vector(0,3) , Sigma );
    
    // likelihoods
    for ( j in 1:N ) {
        Mass[j] ~ normal( alpha[1] + aj[j,1] , M_sd );
        Ripe[j] ~ poisson_log( alpha[2] + aj[j,2] );
        Seed[j] ~ poisson_log( alpha[3] + aj[j,3] );
    }
}

Your first model did indeed take a bit of time on my server but there were are a quite a number of parameters so It wasn't that bad. That being said, to save some time you could try to run the chains in parallel instead of running them in series. Since you are still trying to improve the model you could also run only two chains at a time to save some time and run 4 chains when you'll have a more serious model.

You will also save some time if you use a more sensible number than 1e+05 for the inverse wishart prior. Unlike the other samplers Stan does try to explore the full parameter space and putting really large priors usually result in a really slow adaptive phase. However, if you take some time to browse the help list you'll see that many people don't like the use of the inverse-wishart distribution as a prior so maybe you could try something else.  

Hope this help

Chris

> I suspect what is sought here is a model in which multiple binary outcomes are modeled as correlated through a common matrix of varying intercepts. The intercepts are sampled from a multi_normal, but then pushed through logistic transform to get probabilities for each outcome for each cluster.
>
> For example (the following is not Stan code!):
>
> y1_ij ~ binomial( n1 , p1_ij )
> y2_ij ~ binomial( n2 , p2_ij )
> logit(p1_ij) = a1j
> logit(p2_ij) = a2j
> (a1j,a2j) ~ multi_normal( (a1,a2) , Sigma )
> // + priors
>
> So the outcomes y1,y2 end up correlated through the varying effect matrix, but are different outcome variables. The cluster indexed by j is measured for both y1 and y2.
>
> I was working on something like this recently for a plant biologist, who has thousands of replicate plants and three outcomes measured per plant (possibly repeated at different growth points). One thing of interest is the correlation structure among the outcomes as a function of treatment, so I used something like the above to do it. Here's the basic Stan mode code I used, which might help Vera, or at least clarify the issue. (NB: this code isn't optimized yet. It could be faster, I'm sure.)

>     int Ripe[N];        // outcome variable 2
>     int Seed[N];        // outcome variable 3

>    
>     // plant means
